components.text: Whether sincere, costly belief establishes the truth of the witnesses' supernatural interpretation.
Whether reports of appearance experiences establish that a bodily resurrection actually occurred.
Transformation and costly sincerity establish belief or experience, not the truth of the supernatural interpretation.
Reports that appearances occurred must be distinguished from independent evidence that resurrection caused them.
Whether resurrection is an eligible best-explanation candidate without support that supernatural interaction is possible.
Whether religious context supplies evidence that a supernatural cause can interact with reality.
Resurrection must be shown to be a viable explanatory candidate before it can win a best-explanation comparison.
Evidence must connect supernatural agency to reality rather than exempting it from ordinary standards.
Whether resurrection outranks known mechanisms producing false or exaggerated reports.
Whether labeling God special establishes a viable causal mechanism rather than special pleading.
Known mechanisms producing false reports remain better grounded than an unsupported resurrection mechanism.
Whether late, dependent, and inconsistent accounts securely establish burial and empty-tomb facts.
Whether transmitted appearance accounts are sufficiently early and independent to establish the proposed data.
Whether the cited source base independently verifies the proposed historical foundation.
Late, dependent, and inconsistent accounts do not securely establish burial and empty-tomb facts.
The same source-quality problems weaken the asserted historical status of appearance reports.
The general source objection reaches the proposed fact list but gives little crucifixion-specific analysis.
Whether eliminating selected rivals establishes resurrection as the best explanation under incomplete information.
Whether cumulative comparison warrants belief when relevant information and possible explanations remain unknown.
Eliminating selected rivals cannot establish resurrection when the information and possibility set remain incomplete.
Whether incidental local accuracy gives the Gospel reports evidential value beyond bare unsupported claims.
Whether detailed Palestinian knowledge corroborates source reliability despite proposed lateness.
Accurate Palestinian institutions, geography, and customs provide cumulative corroboration of Gospel historical knowledge.
Incidental accuracy can make a source more credible but does not independently prove resurrection.
Whether supernatural possibility must be independently proved before historical evidence and explanatory fit can be considered.
Whether objections should address the specific nonmiraculous historical premises rather than dismiss the whole case generally.
Whether the case is a two-stage abductive argument rather than bare elimination of rivals.
The proper demand is first to assess ordinary historical facts and then compare resurrection as an explanation.
Case-specific comparison is required rather than rejecting resurrection through generalities alone.
Whether withholding belief for an unmet burden circularly assumes that resurrection or the supernatural cannot occur.
Withholding acceptance for unmet burden does not entail that resurrection is impossible or assume the conclusion.
The cumulative case may be assessed while its conclusion remains unaccepted pending sufficient support.
Whether contemporary or independent evidence verifies Jesus' reported crucifixion and associated narrative claims.
Whether incidental narrative detail overcomes the absence of expected independent reports for conspicuous events.
The crucifixion report lacks contemporary verification and expected independent Roman documentation.
The broader narrative's source reliability is questioned through absent independent reports of conspicuous associated events.
Whether the underlying event reports are independently and contemporaneously verified.
Whether the earliest claim meant bodily resurrection rather than a merely spectral experience.
The decisive demand concerns evidential sufficiency, not whether Paul and early Jews meant bodily resurrection.
Clarifying the content of belief does not establish that the believed bodily event occurred.
Whether establishing Paul's bodily meaning establishes that the reported resurrection actually happened.
Whether Paul's third-party list establishes personal witness attestation and the truth of the appearances.
What Paul believed resurrection meant does not establish that the bodily event actually occurred.
Paul's third-party list does not independently establish that named witnesses personally attested as reported.
Whether confirming that Jesus returned to life identifies God or a supernatural mechanism as the cause.
Whether the event description itself supplies the secondary causal explanation.
Confirmation that Jesus was alive again would not by itself identify how it happened or who caused it.
Even bodily return and divine causal attribution remain distinct evidential questions.
Whether the two-part case supplies support proportionate to bodily resurrection's extraordinariness.
Whether resurrection has sufficient physical, contemporary, and possibility-establishing evidence to be accepted.
Whether clarity that the claim is bodily increases rather than removes its evidential burden.
Considering ordinary historical facts does not remove the need for sufficient support for the extraordinary resurrection conclusion.
Lack of physical, contemporary, and possibility-establishing evidence weakens resurrection as a candidate explanation.
The extraordinary bodily claim requires evidence beyond clarification of what early believers meant.
Whether requiring extraordinary evidence entails an endless demand for further extraordinary support.
Whether preliminary support requirements categorically prevent supernatural explanations from entering consideration.
Treating every extraordinary item of support as a new unsupported extraordinary claim can generate an endless regress.
A burden standard should specify sufficient support without recursively excluding every possible item offered.
Whether proportional evidential strength, rather than recursively extraordinary claims, answers the regress objection.
Whether ordinary historical evidence can suffice only if its cumulative quality overcomes conflicting background beliefs.
Extraordinary evidence denotes quantity and quality scaled to the claim, not endlessly miraculous supporting claims.
Ordinary facts may be considered while their aggregate support must overcome conflicting background evidence.
Whether unresolved textual problems and report-only evidence warrant accepting resurrection as the best explanation.
Whether the cumulative case overcomes the residual uncertainty needed for reasonable belief.
Whether corroborating details overcome unresolved textual problems affecting the central claims.
Unresolved textual problems and evidence limited to reports leave the cumulative case insufficient for reasonable acceptance.
An insufficiently supported candidate cannot be accepted merely because it is offered as an explanation.
Suspension follows from present deficits rather than a categorical refusal to consider evidence.
Whether accumulated historical research permits thoughtful present assessment rather than evidential suspension.
Whether lack of direct modern access makes first-century events effectively uninvestigable.
Whether gathered historical data and research can support assessment despite source age.
Accumulated first-century data and later historical research permit thoughtful modern investigation rather than categorical agnosticism.
Modern investigation can assess surviving ancient evidence despite lack of direct contemporary access.
